IdeaLens: Detecting AI Ideas in Long-form Writing

Rishanth Rajendhran Minjoon Choi Jenna Russell Ramya Namuduri    Deniz Bölöni-Turgut  Marzena Karpinska  John Wieting  Mohit Iyyer University of Maryland  Google DeepMind  Simon Fraser University Email: {rishanth, miyyer}@umd.edu  Code |  Models & Data |   Demo
Abstract

While modern AI detectors identify who wrote the words, emerging policies on AI use increasingly hinge on a different question: who came up with the ideas? We introduce IdeaLens, a detector that identifies whether a document’s ideas came from a human or AI (idea provenance), regardless of who wrote its words. To focus IdeaLens on ideas rather than prose, we represent documents as outlines: lists of items that each pair a discourse role with a brief, paraphrased description of the content, minimizing word-level overlap with the raw text. We train IdeaLens on 1M FineWeb documents with silver labels from Pangram, a prose provenance detector. Since the outlines are largely stripped of surface-level information, the labels must be fit mainly through the ideas. In a controlled study, IdeaLens’s AI flag rate drops from 95% to 7% as models write from increasingly detailed human plans, while Pangram 4 still flags 92%; from AI-derived plans, IdeaLens stays above 96%. Conversely, on a new dataset of 50 stories that human authors wrote from AI-generated plans, IdeaLens flags 68% of the stories as AI, compared to 8% for Pangram 4. On a comprehensive suite of 19 existing detection benchmarks, we show that IdeaLens maintains strong detection rates at low false positive rates, suggesting that ideas themselves provide a powerful discriminative signal, and its performance holds across domains, formats, and languages. Finally, we examine 90K predictions from IdeaLens to characterize systematic differences between human and AI ideation. We release our models and labeled datasets to facilitate future research on idea provenance detection.

1 Introduction

In August 2026, the AI detector Pangram flagged a Wall Street Journal op-ed (druckenmiller2026bond) by billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller as 100% AI-generated, to which Druckenmiller unapologetically responded: “Of course I used AI” (stein2026druckenmiller). Paul Gigot, the editor of WSJ’s editorial pages, defended Druckenmiller by arguing that what matters is whether an op-ed “reflects an author’s original argument” and that “nobody can doubt that his op-ed is his genuine opinion” (wapo2026wsjai), though he provided no supporting evidence from the writing process (e.g., chat logs). Detectors like Pangram answer only who wrote the words (prose provenance), while Gigot’s defense, like many emerging policies on AI use in writing (springernature2026ai; iclr2027aipolicy), hinges on who came up with the ideas (idea provenance).11 1 IdeaLens flags the op-ed’s ideas as AI-generated, with P(AI) of 98.3%98.3\% against a decision threshold of 86.3%. This is a model prediction and of course does not constitute direct evidence of the writing process.

Idea and prose provenance can differ within the same document: a human can brainstorm the ideas for a document and ask an AI to write it, or vice versa. Prior work separates the two by building detectors around simulated human–AI collaborations, such as human writing polished by AI or AI writing run through humanizers (Bao2025DecouplingCA; li-etal-2026-beyond-final). These simulations are expensive to create at scale, and detectors trained on them may not transfer to real collaborations. In contrast, prose detectors like Pangram are trained on documents whose ideas and words come from the same source, which are cheap to collect: human text can be sampled from the pre-ChatGPT era, and AI text can be generated on demand.

We propose IdeaLens, an idea provenance detector that learns from the same cheap labels as prose detectors and can therefore be trained at their scale. Our key methodological contribution is to change the classifier’s input. Following the cognitive process model of writing (FlowerHayes1981; hayes2012), we define a document’s ideas as what its author decided to say (e.g., its claims, events, and organization), as opposed to the words used to say it. We represent these ideas as an outline whose items each consist of a discourse role paired with a short description of its content, paraphrased to remove the original wording (Figure 2). We train IdeaLens on a dataset of 1M outlines extracted from FineWeb (penedo2024the) documents, with silver labels from Pangram. As a control, we also train a separate model, ProseLens, with the same backbone, documents, and labels, but on the raw text instead of outlines. Despite identical supervision, the two behave in opposite ways whenever a document’s ideas and words come from different sources, showing that the outline forces IdeaLens to fit the labels through ideas rather than words.

  • •

    IdeaLens detects human ideas in AI-generated documents. On a dataset of AI documents generated from increasingly detailed human plans, IdeaLens’s flag rate falls from 94.9% with minimal human input to 6.8% with a full human outline, while remaining above 96% when plans come instead from AI. ProseLens and Pangram 4 flag 86.5% and 92.4% of documents generated from full human outlines. This behavior is further supported by results on 10 external benchmarks of AI polishing, paraphrasing, and rewriting, where IdeaLens flags 5.6% of documents on average, versus 46.0% for ProseLens and 52.0% for Pangram.

  • •

    IdeaLens detects AI ideas in human writing. The opposite scenario is harder to study: prior work touches on it only through AI text that people or models edit. To this end, we collect the first dataset of long-form documents that people wrote from scratch following AI ideas. Our dataset contains 50 stories, each written from an outline extracted from an AI-generated story, without access to the raw text of that story. IdeaLens flags 68.0% of the human-written stories and 96.0% of the AI originals, while ProseLens and Pangram flag all of the AI original stories but only 0% and 8.0% of the human-written stories, respectively (Figure 1).

  • •

    Despite not seeing the raw text, IdeaLens rivals the strongest open-source detector on conventional benchmarks and transfers across 24 languages. On 19 evaluations that require separating fully AI (ideas and writing) from fully human documents, IdeaLens flags 91.1% of AI documents on average with a false positive rate of 0.6%, compared to 81.8% and 0.2% for EditLens-3B, the strongest existing open-weight detector. ProseLens is even stronger here (98.9% and 0.7%), rivaling the commercial Pangram 4 at its published threshold (97.3% and 0.3%). Although trained only on English, IdeaLens transfers to 24 languages through English outlines, detecting 95.3% of AI documents on average at a false positive rate of 0.1% compared with 82.5% and 0.0% for ProseLens.

  • •

    IdeaLens flags ideas whose details could apply to anything or can’t be verified. Based on an analysis of 90K item-level predictions, we find that IdeaLens scores ideas as more AI when they cite numbers or methods without the context needed to check them, or claim more than their evidence supports. IdeaLens scores ideas as more human when they include specific sources that a reader could look up or discuss downsides and open problems.

We publicly release both IdeaLens and ProseLens along with their training data, the evaluation datasets that we create, and our idea-level analysis.

2 Learning Idea Provenance from Outlines

The fundamental challenge in training an idea detector is that we have no large-scale labels for who came up with a document’s ideas, only for who wrote its prose. Thus, we train on prose labels while replacing each document with an outline that preserves its ideas but not its wording. To create these outlines (Figure 2), we identify discourse roles typical of each writing format, use them to extract an outline of each document, and paraphrase the outline to remove wording copied from the raw document. We train IdeaLens to predict each document’s Pangram label from its paraphrased outline, while ProseLens predicts the same labels from the raw document.

Web documents with silver labels from Pangram.

We sample a 1M subset from WildAI (russell2026aitoken), which labels documents from FineWeb (penedo2024the) with WebOrganizer (wettig2025weborganizer) formats and topics along with authorship labels from Pangram 3.3.2 (thai2026editlens).22 2 We note that Pangram 3.3.2 only provides training labels, while our evaluations benchmark IdeaLens and ProseLens against the more recent Pangram 4. We focus on long-form writing, selecting English documents of at least 500 words that belong to one of eight relevant WebOrganizer formats (), and that Pangram labels as either human-written or AI-generated. We assume that the ideas and prose in these documents share the same source, which enables us to use them as noisy silver labels for idea provenance. We discard documents that Pangram labels as mixed, since AI only wrote part of these texts and thus idea provenance is unclear. We split WildOutlines, the full corpus of 1M documents into training (∼\sim842k), validation (∼\sim30k), calibration (∼\sim80k, human documents only)33 3 The calibration split is used to set a threshold for each detector, which turns its predicted probabilities into binary decisions (AI vs. human). Because the calibration split only contains human-written documents, we can set the threshold to achieve a target false positive rate (FPR). Unless explicitly stated otherwise, we report detector accuracy at thresholds calibrated for an FPR of 1%. and test (∼\sim50k) sets ().44 4 Building the corpus cost about $66.4k (§).

Outlines of discourse roles.

Cognitive models of writing (FlowerHayes1981; hayes2012) separate the act of planning from the act of translating these plans into prose. To build a document representation of the former without the latter, we turn to discourse theory, which describes the roles a passage plays within the broader context of the document, for example through rhetorical structure theory (MANNTHOMPSON+1988+243+281; Mann2006). We represent a document as an outline: an ordered list of discourse roles, each paired with brief descriptions of how those roles are implemented in the document. For example, the op-ed displayed in Figure 2 contains 17 items, starting with an Event Account of a Treasury announcement followed by an Evaluation of the market’s reaction. Many of these roles are format-specific (swales1990genre; SunWangXiong+2021+599+624; van2019macrostructures); for instance, creative writing uses different roles than nonfiction. Thus, we induce separate role sets for each of the eight formats in our dataset ().

Automatically extracting outlines.

We build a training dataset, WildOutlines, for IdeaLens by converting documents to outlines in three automated steps:

  1. (i)

    Role induction: We adapt the TopicGPT framework (pham2024topicgptpromptbasedtopicmodeling) by prompting GPT-5.6 Sol (openai2026gpt56) to propose base roles for each format given a detailed description of that format. Then, we label outlines of 200 documents in that format using those roles, while asking the model to invent new roles as needed. Afterwards, we deduplicate and prune the resulting role set (e.g., to 42 roles for nonfiction); more details in §.

  2. (ii)

    Outline extraction: Given a document, we prompt Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini2023; gemini37flash; gemini31pro) with its format’s role set (and few-shot demonstrations from the much more powerful Claude Fable 5 (anthropic2026fable5)) to produce an outline of the document’s ideas in order, where each item consists of a role and a short content description.

  3. (iii)

    Paraphrasing: Extracted outlines can copy phrasing from the original document, which a model could use as a stylistic shortcut to the label (i.e., human wording can leak into the outlines). Therefore, we prompt Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini31pro) to paraphrase each outline. This pushes all outlines toward a homogeneous, AI-like style: for human-written documents, the fraction of outline text that Pangram 4 labels as human drops from 8.5% to 0.3% (). Meaning is still preserved (), as paraphrased outlines have a cosine similarity of 0.93 with the originally extracted outlines (vs. 0.39 for unrelated outlines) and 0.76 with the source document (vs. 0.26). We paraphrase only for training, to keep the model from learning style; at inference, IdeaLens sees the unparaphrased outline.

Training IdeaLens and ProseLens.

Both of our models start from a backbone of Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (nvidia2026nemotron35lightning), fine-tuned for one epoch with LoRA (hu2022lora) using Tinker (tml2026tinker).55 5 Details and results for other backbones are in §. We threshold each model’s probability that a document is AI-generated at a 1% false positive rate on our calibration split. The only difference between the two models is that IdeaLens is trained on paraphrased outlines, whereas ProseLens is trained on the original documents. Since they share their backbone, training documents, and labels, any difference in their behavior is a direct result of transforming the input into our outline representation.

3 Experimental setup

We evaluate IdeaLens and ProseLens against 17 existing detectors, including the state-of-the-art Pangram 4, on 19 external benchmarks and three datasets that we create ourselves: IdeaShift, IdeaShift-X, and TwiceTold. These datasets cover all four quadrants in Figure 1: documents with shared provenance (fully human or fully AI) as well as documents with mixed provenance (human ideas and AI prose, or AI ideas and human prose). Idea detectors should achieve high accuracy in all four quadrants, while prose detectors should fail in the two mixed quadrants.

Evaluation metrics and baselines.

We report accuracy at detecting AI ideas, which we define as the percentage of documents whose predicted label (AI or human) agrees with the source of their ideas. Our baselines include Pangram 4 (glickenhaus2026pangram4technicalreport), EditLens-Llama-3.2-3B (thai2026editlens), Fast-DetectGPT (bao2024fastdetectgpt), Binoculars (hans2024spotting), MELD (li2026meldmultitaskequilibratedlearning) and Desklib (desklib2025aitextdetector). For IdeaLens, ProseLens, and EditLens, we set a global threshold across all formats at 1% FPR on our calibration set. We binarize Pangram’s ternary labels (AI, AI-assisted, human) following its tech report, and other baselines use their default thresholds.66 6 Details on thresholding, including the Pangram conversion, are in §.

Existing benchmarks.

Of the 19 external detection benchmarks (see § for full list), 14 contain documents with shared provenance (fully human or fully AI). We evaluate accuracy on these documents and on our in-domain test set of 50K documents from our Pangram-labeled web corpus. We also measure FPR on a set of 10K documents from C4 (c4dataset), which was created prior to ChatGPT’s release and is thus much more likely to be human-written than our silver-labeled test set. Finally, 10 external benchmarks also contain documents written by humans but edited by an AI (e.g., via paraphrasing, polishing, or rewriting), which we use as instances of human ideas rendered in AI prose; this includes OpAI-Bench (Bsharat2026OperationGuidedPH) and GEDE (Gehring2025LimitsOL).

IdeaShift: AI writing from increasingly detailed human plans.

A common collaborative writing pattern is for a human to give an AI their ideas via a prompt, which it uses to write a document from scratch (10.1145/3698061.3726910). Only two external datasets we evaluate on contain instances of this pattern (saha2026policies; Gehring2025LimitsOL), and neither controls the amount of human input, so it is unclear how much of the final document’s ideas came from the human. Thus, we create IdeaShift from 500 seed documents (both human-written and AI-generated) sampled from our in-domain test set. For each seed document, GPT-5.6 Sol (openai2026gpt56) writes five progressively more detailed prompts: the level-0 prompt contains only the topic (e.g., “Write a dining and lifestyle blog post reviewing a restaurant visit.”), while the level-5 prompt contains the full outline extracted as per §2 with instructions to add nothing else to it. GPT-5.6 models then generate a new document for each prompt. Since all of the prose in IdeaShift is AI-generated, prose detectors should flag every document as AI, and an idea detector should do the same for AI seeds. However, on documents generated from human seeds, idea detectors should flag fewer and fewer documents as the prompts carry more of the human plan.

TwiceTold: humans writing from AI plans.

We are also interested in the reverse pattern: a human obtains ideas from an AI and then writes the document themselves. Existing datasets approximate this pattern with AI-generated text that humans edit or AI tools humanize,77 7 E.g., LAMP (LAMP), HART (Bao2025DecouplingCA), and baumler-etal-2026-make. but these edited documents are still largely AI-generated and thus do not cleanly separate idea and prose provenance. To fill this gap, we create TwiceTold,88 8 Named after Twice-Told Tales, a collection of previously published short stories by Nathaniel Hawthorne. a dataset with 50 stories written from scratch by humans given only the outline of a 500-word story generated by GPT-5.6 Sol (see § for more details).99 9 The stories were written in person by 17 computer science graduate students or faculty. We avoided crowdsourcing to reduce the chance of AI use during the writing process (10.1145/3685527). Prose detectors should label these stories as human, while idea detectors should label them as AI. We also include the 50 original AI stories, which all detectors should label as AI.

IdeaShift-X: idea detection in multilingual documents.

While prose detectors rely on language-specific features (e.g., vocabulary choice, sentence structure), IdeaLens uses an LLM extractor that can generate English outlines for documents in any language. Thus, even though IdeaLens is trained only on English documents, we can apply it to documents in other languages without any additional training. To test this, we create IdeaShift-X by sampling 10K human-authored documents in 24 languages () from FineWeb2 (penedo2025fineweb), to measure FPR across different languages. For each, we follow the IdeaShift protocol to generate AI versions in the original language at level 0 (AI ideas) and level 5 (human ideas).

4 IdeaLens detects AI ideas, not AI prose

footnote 11summarizes our main results across 51 evaluation splits from 22 benchmarks, where each point is a detector plotted by its aggregate idea detection accuracy on documents with shared vs. mixed provenance. IdeaLens is the only detector that achieves high accuracy in both shared (95.3%) and mixed (81.3%) settings. ProseLens and Pangram 4 are extremely accurate on documents with shared provenance (99.1% and 98.5%, respectively) but fail to identify the source of a document’s ideas in mixed settings (25.4% and 25.9%). Since ProseLens has the same backbone, training documents, and training labels as IdeaLens, this highlights the impact of our outline representation, which a ModernBERT-based pair (warner-etal-2025-smarter) replicates with a different backbone. IdeaLens also transfers unexpectedly well to raw text inputs at test time, exhibiting high shared provenance accuracy and substantially higher mixed provenance accuracy than ProseLens.

IdeaLens detects idea provenance on IdeaShift.

As the human plan in the prompts from IdeaShift becomes more detailed, IdeaLens’s flag rate drops from 94.9% at level 0 to 6.8% at level 5 (4(a)). In contrast, ProseLens and Pangram 4 flag 86–100% of documents regardless of the level of human ideation. When the plans come from AI instead of humans, IdeaLens consistently flags more than 96% of documents at every level (), showing that it is sensitive to idea provenance rather than level of prompt detail. Finally, we observe that the biggest drop in flag rate occurs between levels 3 and 4, which is when the prompts begin including outlines with content in addition to structural role information ().

IdeaLens is insensitive to AI rewording of human ideas.

Aggregated over 12 benchmarks where AI makes surface-level changes to human text (e.g., polishing, paraphrasing), IdeaLens labels 94.7% of documents as human, compared to 50.7% for ProseLens and 43.8% for Pangram 4 (). In GEDE (Gehring2025LimitsOL), IdeaLens flags only 0.5% of human essays as AI after minor corrections made by an LLM (vs Pangram 4’s 54.6% and ProseLens’s 45.8%) and 2.6% after a rewrite preserving the original content (vs Pangram 4’s 94.3% and ProseLens’s 77.1%). In HART (Bao2025DecouplingCA), IdeaLens flags 4.9% of LLM paraphrases of human documents, compared to 42.8% by Pangram 4 and 44.5% by ProseLens. In the Academic Integrity dataset (Karr2026WhyAD), it flags 8.2% of abstracts that an LLM generated from a human-written reference abstract, compared to Pangram 4’s 96.4% and ProseLens’s 83.9%.

IdeaLens detects AI ideas in TwiceTold’s human-written prose.

IdeaLens flags 68% (95% CI 54–79%) of TwiceTold stories as AI, compared to 0% for ProseLens and 8% for Pangram 4.1212 12 Pangram 4’s flags are likely due to usage of character names typical of AI writing (e.g., Mara, Bellweather). All detectors are reliable at flagging the AI-generated original stories (96% for IdeaLens and 100% for ProseLens and Pangram), but only IdeaLens sticks with its prediction for the majority of the human stories, even though the prose is completely different (4(b)). The stories that IdeaLens marks as human generally follow their outlines while adding new events or world-building details: 12 out of 16 errors are on stories that contain speculative or fantasy elements.

From ideas alone, IdeaLens outperforms the strongest existing open detectors.

On 19 evaluation splits with shared provenance, IdeaLens detects 91.1% of AI documents at 0.6% FPR compared with 81.8% at 0.2% FPR for EditLens-3B,1313 13 While IdeaLens’s 30B backbone is larger than EditLens-3B, it is a mixture-of-experts model with only 3B active parameters. Our IdeaLens-ModernBERT variant, with only 0.4B parameters, detects 79.1% of AI documents at an FPR of 1.5%. the strongest existing open baseline (), with both calibrated to a 1% target. Training on full text does better: ProseLens reaches 98.9% at 0.7% FPR, rivaling Pangram 4 (97.3% at 0.3%) and making it the strongest open detector in our evaluations. To cleanly measure FPR, we collect 10K pre-ChatGPT documents from C4: IdeaLens flags only 0.01% compared to 0% for ProseLens and Pangram 4 (§). Against humanization and adversarial attacks, IdeaLens’s detection rate drops 6.4 points on average, between Pangram’s 4.9 and ProseLens’s 10.6 (). One weakness of IdeaLens is DIPPER paraphrasing (krishna2023paraphrasing) in GEDE (Gehring2025LimitsOL), where it detects 77.6% versus 97.1% for ProseLens and 95.1% for Pangram 4; we suspect this attack changes content as well as style (§).

IdeaLens detects idea provenance across 24 languages on IdeaShift-X.

IdeaShift-X contains documents generated in 24 different languages, and IdeaLens flags 95.3% of the level-0 documents but only 0.7% of the level-5 documents despite being trained only on English. These results show that signatures of AI ideas are largely invariant to the language in which they are written. In contrast, prose detectors like ProseLens and Pangram 4 flag 82–85% of level-0 and 45–62% of level-5 documents, and this gap between IdeaLens and these detectors widens in low-resource languages like Tamil and Amharic. Additionally, IdeaLens achieves a low FPR on non-English human-written documents: on 10K pre-ChatGPT documents in these 24 languages sampled from FineWeb2 (penedo2025fineweb), it flags only 0.1% as AI ().
